extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, critics, and practitioners of poetry and drama (readers of Aristotelian poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle-derived criteria for composing and evaluating poetry (especially tragedy): means/objects/manner of imitation, plot and character requirements, catharsis, unities, diction, music, and practical craft rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the common principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry and Tragedy, Comedy also and dithyrambic poetry, and the greater part of the music of the flute and of the lyre, are all in their general conception modes of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats imitation as the defining principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture; he emphasises that imitation is not mere literal copying but representation of persons acting, with emphasis on how the medium shapes the imitation. (See repeated assertion that the arts 'perform imitation' and that poetry is an expression of the universal.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of imitation: rhythm, language, and harmony (melody)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the arts above mentioned, taken as a whole, the imitation is produced by rhythm, language, and 'harmony,' either singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different arts employ different means: flute and lyre use melody and rhythm, dancing uses rhythm alone, and poetry uses language (prose or verse) either alone or combined with rhythm and melody (as in tragedy and comedy). Which means are employed determines formal differences between arts and genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: character, emotion (πάθη), action
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are persons acting, and these persons must be either of a higher or a lower type; in poetry these are commonly character, emotion (πάθη), and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish types represented (better, worse, or as they are). Tragedy aims to represent men 'better' than in actual life, Comedy 'worse', and other arts vary likewise. Choice of object/type is a primary basis for genre differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: dramatic, narrative, or mixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form either dramatic, narrative (including lyric poetry), or pure drama; manners of imitation differ (e.g., Homer narrates, drama imitates action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manner of presentation (whether the poet recounts or represents action directly) affects the effect and genre classification; the same material may be treated differently according to manner (dramatic enactment vs narrative report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal (τὸ καθόλου)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is an expression of the 'universal'; that is, of the universal element in human life — an idealised image of character, emotion, action under forms manifest to sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is 'a more philosophical and higher thing than History' because it represents universals through particulars. The poet's truth is not empirical detail but the portrayal of probable or necessary human types and events that reveal the universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (mythos) is the primary element of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (μῦθος) or Action (πρᾶξις) is the primary element according to Aristotle: the representation of the action is of primary importance; character and thought come next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good plot must be a whole, complete in itself, of a certain magnitude; plots should be organised as an organic unity (beginning, middle, end). Other elements (character, diction, thought, spectacle, song) are subordinate to the needs of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (primary unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Action is the primary unity; unity consists not in the hero but in unity of action: the parts must be organically connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should present a single connected action; subordinate or episodic incidents that don't contribute to the central action weaken the work. Unity of action is the central organizing principle for dramatic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (continuity of time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity (ἐς Continuity) 'of Time': the prevailing practice of the Greek stage, as incidentally noted by Aristotle; afterwards made into a rule of dramatic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes the practice of attempting to coincide the time of the action with the time of representation (single revolution), but treats unity of time as less primary than unity of action; time-unity is often a practical constraint derived from dramatic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Place
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Place is suggested as consequential to unity of time and sometimes deduced from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of place is not an absolute necessity but tends to follow from concentration of action in time; Aristotle treats unity of place as often subordinate to the higher unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (κάθαρσις) of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic Katharsis of pity and fear: the medical metaphor. The Katharsis implies not only an emotional release but a clearing or clarifying of emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy's effect is to produce and then clarify pity and fear in the audience; catharsis is connected with the representation of the universal rather than mere sensational arousal. Reliance on spectacle alone to produce these emotions is seen as against the spirit of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic protagonist (ideal type) requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal type of protagonist is deduced by Aristotle from the function of Tragedy to produce pity and fear; certain types of characters are excluded (e.g., pure villainy or purely perfect virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragic hero should be neither wholly good nor wholly bad but of a kind to evoke pity and fear—capable of a reversal consistent with human plausibility. Aristotle's rules are tentative; some noble figures may not fit his requisites, but the general principle guides selection of protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia) and Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden Reversal of Fortune (περιπέτεια) and Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις) are key devices in complex plots; together they produce the tragic or disastrous incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that include peripeteia and anagnorisis achieve stronger tragic effects because they show a necessary and probable change in the hero's fortune arising from the plot's incidents, heightening pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity (rule of sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry excludes the rule of Chance. The rule of probable or necessary sequence as to the incidents is essential; certain plots are condemned for want of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents should follow from one another by necessity or probability; implausible or purely accidental events weaken poetic credibility. The best tragic effects combine the inevitable with the unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple versus Complex plot distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of Simple (ἁπλοῖ) and Complex (σύνθετα) Plots: complex plots include reversal and recognition, simple plots do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple plot has a single movement without peripeteia or anagnorisis; complex plots that incorporate those elements are generally superior for producing catharsis but must still preserve unity and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, chorus, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'quantitative parts' (μέρη κατὰ τὸ ποσόν) of Tragedy are defined: Prologue, Episode, Stasimon (choral ode), Exodus, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of these parts helps organisation of the play; Aristotle remarks some passages on parts may be interpolated, but the general schema (prologue, episodes, choral odes integrated into the whole) is normative. Choral odes should be organic to the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (διάνοια) and Diction (λέξις) as dramatic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (διάνοια), the intellectual element, and Diction (λέξις) are elements of tragedy: thought may be expressed by dramatic speeches or through incidents; diction is primarily the art of declamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought should arise naturally from the plot and characters; diction must balance elevation and perspicuity. Rhetorical rules govern speeches, while poetic diction permits metaphor and stylistic devices appropriate to the medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: admissible language and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic diction: the words and modes of speech admissible in Poetry, including Metaphor in particular; poetry combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of metaphor and elevated modes is allowed, but clarity must be maintained. Certain grammatical or lexical interpolations in manuscript tradition are noted as corrupt; practical guidance is to employ language that fits character and maintains intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music (μελοποιία) and Song as elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Song (μελοποιία) and musical elements are among the constituents of tragedy and are substantial artistic components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music contributes to katharsis and the unity of the work; it should be integrated artistically. Different poetic genres combine melody, rhythm, and metre in varying proportions—recognise how music interrelates with language and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (ὄψις) and its limited artistic role
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenic Presentment (ὄψεως κόσμος), i.e., spectacle, is one of the six elements but is not central: to produce pity and fear by Stage Spectacle alone is contrary to the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle is the least artistic element (most mechanical); reliance on visual shock rather than plot and character is an anti-pattern. Spectacle may amplify but should not substitute for properly arranged action and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcharging tragedy with epic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry; tragic composition requires economy compared with epic's wider canvas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce excessive narrative digressions, elaborated description, or episodic material better suited to epic length; maintain unity and immediacy suitable to the dramatic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical craft rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules: (1) To place the scene before his eyes and to act the parts himself to enter into vivid sympathy; (2) To sketch the bare outline of the action before filling in episodes; (3) Care about complication and dénouement; (4) Unite varied forms of excellence; (5) Make choral odes organic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are compositional heuristics: rehearsal/embodiment aids empathic writing; outline ensures coherent structure; careful handling of complication and denouement secures probability and catharsis; integrate chorus and variety without disrupting unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth versus common (historical) truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic Truth: the meaning of Poetic Truth and its difference from common reality; poetry speaks the probable and the possible rather than the strictly factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses to critics arguing poetry misrepresents reality: Aristotle defends poets by distinguishing poetic (universal) truth from literal historical accuracy. Poetic plausibility and moral/psychological truth matter more than factual exactitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as the end of Fine Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Fine Art is pleasure. Lower forms afford the pleasure of a pastime; its higher forms, that noble enjoyment (διαγωγή) which belongs to supreme happiness (εὐδαιμονία).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art's value is aesthetic pleasure, which ranges from light amusement to deep, edifying enjoyment connected to human flourishing. The spectator's pleasure is an essential criterion of artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between aesthetic and moral/educational function
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes the educational from the aesthetic function of Poetry; his critical estimates rest on purely aesthetic grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ancient tradition ascribed moral instruction to poetry, Aristotle cautions that critical judgment should focus on artistic merits (unity, imitation, catharsis) though moral effects are not ignored; avoid conflating didactic aims with purely formal aesthetic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's generalising power and differing idealisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an example of the universalising faculty of Poetry; comedy idealises life in a different way from tragedy, representing men as worse than in actual life and creating sportive ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise differences in how comedy and tragedy idealise (comic generalisation versus tragic idealisation). In modern drama the boundary is less sharp; humour and pathos may intermingle, but each genre's aims and methods remain distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myth and historic material to achieve poetic universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry uses myth or heroic history as a chief means by which poets ascend from the individual to the universal; myth fuses truth and fiction to provide the idealising medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting and shaping mythic/historical material allows the poet to lift particular events into archetypal significance. Employ collective or traditional material to achieve the imaginative remoteness that reveals universal human traits.
